The 4th grade.

I'd had my doubts for a while, I mean, Santa Claus wasn't real, and my parents had long revealed the secret to the "Easter Bunny footprints," trick, so the next natural thing for me to start doubting was God. When my nana's lung cancer took a turn for the worst, I got down on my knees next to my mother and father and my sisters and I prayed. I prayed harder than I ever had - I prayed for healing, I prayed to have my nana back home from the hospital, I prayed for a doctor with a miracle cure - I prayed for anything but death, and I believed in my heart that the combined prayers of my family would reach His divine ears. A few weeks later, my nana passed away - her passing made all the more cruel by her seeming return to health just days before another drastic turn for the worst and her passing.

"God brought her home to end her suffering." "She doesn't have to hurt anymore." "God works in mysterious ways." "Her pain is gone now." Each sentiment more offensive to my mind than the last. Her pain is gone? No, it's not gone - it just moved to someone else. Her pain became my pain, our pain.

God had let me down - had let us down. We prayed for mercy and were given the rod. Either He didn't exist, He didn't care, or He was outright malevolent.

Somewhere between middle and high school.

I was raised Catholic, and I started thinking about things for myself. I was asking questions about incest and Adam & Eve, why God allowed slavery and rape, or other contradictions I found in the Bible. Whenever I asked, I was told to shut up, and I just slumped over and went on with my day.

One school day, a new kid joined my group of friends, and we were kind of introducing ourselves, and a close friend told the new kid that he (the close friend) and I were atheists... I was stunned for a second, thought about it for a second, and felt the confusion just slide. From then on i've just accepted it. It's easier to think logically than to suppress that logic for a god that I have never seen, heard, or have any proof of.

It's not so much that I wholeheartedly believe "Oh, there is no God", as much as I consider it functionally irrelevant. If I were to wake up tomorrow and see irrefutable proof one way or the other, neither one would substantially change my life. I do my sincere best to live a good, kind life because I enjoy who I am as a person when I live this way. I don't need more than that.

This is called apatheism and it is the most reasonable position to me.

I also like ignosticism, the viewpoint that the question of whether or not God exists isn't well-defined, because we don't have a satisfying enough definition of God, and perhaps such a satisfying definition isn't possible.
